vignette:
It happened two years ago, on a Tuesday afternoon in late spring. He had taken the bus home from work, something he did every day, and was walking through the central market to pick up vegetables for dinner. That part of the city was always crowded-vendors calling out prices, the smell of fried noodles and diesel exhaust, children weaving between shoppers. He remembers hearing a loud crack, then a roar that seemed to swallow everything. The ground shook. He was thrown forward, his palms scraping against concrete. For a long moment there was only dust, a ringing in his ears, and then the screaming began.

He lay still, face down, afraid to move. When he finally lifted his head, he saw a man's shoe a few feet away, still laced, with no one inside it. There was blood on the pavement, the metal frames of market stalls twisted like wire. He crawled behind a collapsed table and stayed there until emergency workers found him, trembling and silent. He was not physically hurt beyond scrapes and a bruised rib, but he cannot forget the sound-that wet, percussive thud, then the silence before the screams.

In the weeks after, he stopped taking the bus. He avoided the market entirely, taking a longer route that added thirty minutes to his commute. At first his wife understood. She held him when he woke up gasping from nightmares, his sheets soaked in sweat. But the nightmares didn't stop, and he started sleeping on the couch so he wouldn't disturb her. He became irritable, snapping at small things-a dropped spoon, the television volume too high. He stopped wanting to go out on weekends. Crowds made his heart race, his palms sweat. Even a full restaurant felt like a trap.

He is now 26, divorced for eight months. His wife left after he spent an entire weekend staring at the wall, not speaking, afraid to leave the apartment. He understood. He couldn't blame her.

At work as a bank teller, he does his best to manage. The bank is quiet, with a heavy glass barrier between him and the customers, and that helps. But there are triggers he cannot predict. A customer's raised voice-impatience over a slow transaction-makes his chest tighten. A sudden slam of the door from the back office sends him upright in his chair, heart hammering. He has learned to anticipate the lunch rush. The line of people pressing forward, their faces impatient, reminds him of the market that day, the way the crowd seemed to push him closer to the blast. He sometimes excuses himself to the break room, locks the door, and breathes slowly until his hands stop shaking.

His manager has noticed he flinches at loud noises, but he doesn't explain. He just says he gets headaches. At home, he keeps the curtains drawn. He does not watch the news. He does not answer calls from his family, who live in another city. He feels hollow, disconnected, as though he is watching his own life from a great distance. When he counts cash at the end of the day, running his thumb over each bill, he sometimes loses track-his mind drifting back to that afternoon, the dust in his lungs, the man's shoe.

He has not told anyone the full story. He does not talk about how he sometimes sees fragments of it in the reflection of the bank's glass doors, or how the smell of diesel exhaust still makes him nauseous. He goes to work, comes home, eats a frozen dinner, and lies in bed waiting for sleep or for the alarm, whichever comes first.
